summary: Bulk license transfer triggers missing prorated credit after rate-ladder re-evaluation
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports a missing prorated credit after transferring 1200 reserved seats from cost-center A to cost-center B. The transfer occurred mid-billing-cycle and coincided with an automated rate-ladder re-evaluation.

Impact: BrightPath sees a ~$28k charge on the finalized invoice that they expect to be reduced by an applied prorated reserved-credit. Customer is enterprise and reported outage risk for finance reconciliation.

Environment: Production, us-east region, enterprise plan with reserved capacity and negotiated per-model overrides. Transfer executed from Console > Billing > Transfer Licenses bulk UI.

Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Navigate to Console > Billing > Organizations > Cost Centers.
2) Select cost-center-A (source) and choose "Transfer seats" to cost-center-B (destination).
3) Transfer 1200 seats on 2026-03-05 22:05 UTC mid-billing-cycle.
4) Rate-ladder re-evaluation job ran automatically at 2026-03-05 22:10 UTC.
5) Final invoice generated 2026-03-06 shows full reserved-hour line on source and no prorated credit for transferred seats.

Observed behavior: No prorated credit line computed for the 1200 seats on the source cost-center; destination appears to have reserved-hours credited immediately but invoicing system did not emit a negative prorate line for the source. Console shows transfer completed. Billing export postbacks show a rate-selector tag at time-of-transfer that differs from the rate cache used by the hourly-prorate worker.

Expected behavior: Transfer should create a prorated negative line on source and a prorated positive allocation to destination so net charge reflects only time each cost-center held the reserved seats.

Logs/attachments customer provided: billing_export_2026-03-06.csv, console_screens_2026-03-05.png, transfer_audit_log_excerpt.txt, invoice_2026-03-06.pdf.

Requested outcome: Apply missing prorated credit to customer's invoice or provide credit memo and explain root cause. Customer requests an ETA for remediation and a postmortem for process changes to prevent reoccurrence.

investigation_notes:
Hypotheses: 1) Race between bulk-transfer finalization and rate-ladder re-evaluation leading to inconsistent rate tag at time of hourly-prorate calculation. 2) Transfer bulk UI path emitted event schema variant missing prorate_marker/seat_count causing reconciler to skip source adjustment.

Queries executed: SQL reconcile_reserved_transfers_v2 by transfer_uuid -> showed rows with NULL prorate_marker for this UUID. Hourly-prorate worker logs (2026-03-05T22:05:00Z - 22:20:00Z) show two events: transfer.apply and rate-ladder.refresh; order differs across shards.

Related artifacts: github.com/redwood/reconciler/pull/1482 (partial fix), slack: #billing-incidents message link https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C02BILL/p16324, confluence runbook at /display/BILL/Prorate+Ladder+Spec.

Immediate mitigations considered: 1) Run one-off reconciler backfill for affected transfers in time window 2026-03-05T21:55 - 22:30. 2) Add idempotency and schema validation to transfer event producer. 3) Short-term: issue manual credit memo while hotfix deployed.
resolution:
Workaround and remediation plan in progress. Short-term: Manual credit memo being prepared for BrightPath (draft ready 2026-03-14). Medium-term: Deploy reconciler consumer fix to accept legacy schema variant and perform canonical lookup of transfer-audit stream. Long-term: Add transactional locking or ordering guarantees between rate-ladder re-eval and transfer-finalize flows.

Follow-ups:
- Backfill job to run against affected window (owner: Tomás Rivera) due 2026-03-15.
- Post-incident RCA and change to transfer UI event schema required (owner: Product Eng).
- Add automated billing integration tests for bulk-transfer mid-cycle (owner: QA).

Closure criteria: credit memo issued and customer confirms invoice is reconciled; reconciler consumer fix deployed and backfill completes without new missing-prorate cases in the subsequent billing cycle.
